tldr: This research turns everyday household tools into interchangeable robot end effectors using sub-$10 3D-printed adapters and tactile sensors, enabling delicate cooking and other complex contact-rich tasks through tactile-feedback teleoperation and imitation learning.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the SwapBot system. The left shows the robot arm equipped with electromagnetic coupling and a tool rack; the center shows the multi-layer structure of the piezoresistive tactile sensor and its placement on various tools; the right shows the load response characteristics across different electrode widths.
overview:
When humans cook, they skillfully swap tools depending on the job—slicing with a knife, spreading sauce with a brush, or grabbing ingredients with tongs. In current robotics research, however, the dominant approaches rely either on a single expensive and complex dexterous multi-fingered hand, or on forcing a simple two-finger parallel gripper to grasp tools. The former is notoriously difficult to control and maintain, while the latter struggles with tasks requiring delicate force modulation like cutting or spreading. Both suffer from the same fundamental issue: a lack of tactile feedback directly at the contact interface.

Inspired by surgical robots that smoothly swap between scissors and forceps, the authors asked: "Rather than building a universal human-like hand, why not autonomously swap tools and sense touch directly at the tool tip?" This led to the development of SwapBot. By attaching low-cost adapters (under $10 each) and custom thin-film tactile sensors to off-the-shelf everyday tools, they built a mechanism capable of autonomous swapping in about 10 seconds via electromagnetic coupling. Furthermore, they created an intuitive teleoperation system where the operator manipulates the exact same tool as the robot, making high-quality demonstration collection easy.

In experiments, the system tackled a long-horizon, contact-rich task: cooking pan-fried tofu (brushing sauce onto fragile tofu, transferring it to a pan with tongs, returning it to a cutting board, and slicing it with a knife). Training a Diffusion Policy augmented with tactile feedback boosted success rates by 15–25 percentage points over an RGB-only policy, achieving an overall task completion rate of 60%. This demonstrates that modular, tactile-equipped tools offer a powerful and practical shortcut toward capable robot manipulation.
contributions: Developed a universal interface using low-cost sub-$10 3D-printed adapters and electromagnetic coupling that autonomously swaps both passive tools and articulated tools like tongs in about 10 seconds.

Integrated thin-film tactile sensors made from commercial conductive fabric and piezoresistive film (Velostat) into tool blades and handles, enabling direct measurement of contact forces at the tool tips.
Built an intuitive teleoperation system where the human operator manipulates tools matching the robot's geometry, with real-time tactile feedback overlaid on-screen.

Validated on physical robots that adding tactile feedback to visual inputs significantly improves imitation learning success rates on a delicate pan-fried tofu cooking task, maintaining high performance even with limited demonstration data.

sections.heading: Why Build a Universal Hand When You Can Just Swap Tools?
sections.summary: Handling complex household tasks with a single robotic hand is mechanically and control-wise difficult. SwapBot turns everyday tools into interchangeable end effectors using low-cost adapters with integrated tactile sensors, achieving dexterous and robust tool manipulation.
sections.details:
Everyday robot manipulation in household environments consists of a sequence of diverse actions such as cutting, spreading, and grasping, most of which inherently involve tool use. For instance, a seemingly simple task like "cooking pan-fried tofu" requires delicately brushing sauce without crumbling the tofu, securely grasping and moving it with tongs, and slicing it with a knife under controlled force.

However, conventional robot hand design faces a major dilemma. Anthropomorphic multi-fingered hands are dexterous, but their complex mechanisms lead to high maintenance costs and make control and demonstration collection extremely difficult. On the other hand, widely used parallel-jaw two-finger grippers are easy to handle, yet poorly suited for tasks involving delicate or forceful physical contact like cutting or spreading. Moreover, both approaches lack tactile sensors to directly measure what occurs at the contact interface between the tool and the object, making contact-rich tasks hard to learn.

While industrial tool changers exist for CNC machines or UR robots, they are prohibitively expensive, custom-designed for specific robots, and cannot support articulated tools requiring actuation (opening and closing mechanisms) like tongs or scissors. Taking inspiration from surgical robots that interchange instruments for specific tasks, this study chose to solve manipulation challenges through "tool diversity" rather than complicating hand mechanics.

The proposed system, SwapBot, converts everyday items into robot tools using inexpensive 3D-printed parts costing only around $10, enabling autonomous swapping in under 10 seconds via electromagnetic coupling. Furthermore, compact piezoresistive tactile sensors are integrated into each tool, and an intuitive teleoperation system using human-matched tools enables high-quality demonstration collection. The system mounts onto three distinct robot arms—Franka, UR5, and Tycho—demonstrating cross-platform versatility across robot models.

captions.F3: SwapBot mounted on three different robot arms: Tycho, UR5, and Franka. The standardized robot-side interface allows swapping and using diverse tools regardless of the robot arm model.

sections.heading: Low-Cost Hardware Coupling Meets a Hierarchical Policy
sections.summary: SwapBot combines sub-$10 adapters and electromagnetic coupling, tool-customized thin tactile sensors, an intuitive teleoperation interface, and a hierarchical learning framework pairing high-level tool selection with low-level diffusion policies.
sections.details:
SwapBot consists of four main components:

### II-A Modular End-Effector: Tool Adapters and Coupling Mechanism
The design goals are an extremely low cost of under $10 per unit, easy assembly with basic tools like an Allen key, and fast tool swapping across diverse robots. The tool-side skeleton is 3D printed with PLA, and soft silicone is cast between the tool handle and the adapter. This allows the same adapter to accommodate variations in handle thickness and shape.
When driving articulated tools that require opening and closing (such as tongs or chopsticks), mounting individual motors on each tool would make them heavy and expensive. Therefore, all actuation is centralized on the robot arm side. The system converts the rotational torque of the arm's wrist joint into the opening/closing motion of the tool via bearings; for robots lacking a wrist roll joint, a single compact servo motor is added. For tool attachment and detachment, a self-aligning coupling combines electromagnets with mechanical guide gears, reliably completing tool swapping at the dock in about 10 seconds even with minor misalignments.

### II-B Compact Tactile Sensing: Instrumented Tools
To capture contact states, a custom three-layer piezoresistive tactile sensor was created by sandwiching pressure-sensitive conductive film (Velostat) between laser-cut conductive fabric electrodes. Pressure is detected at the intersections (grid) of orthogonal rows and columns, allowing an $n \times n$ sensor array to be wired with just $2n$ lines.
For tools with large contact areas like knives and tongs, sensors are attached to both the blade/tip and the handle. For tools with slender tips like brushes or chopsticks where tip mounting is difficult, sensors are placed on the handle to indirectly estimate contact forces. The handle sensors are sandwiched between an outer TPU layer and silicone, ensuring stable output without compromising grip feel.

### II-C Teleoperation Interface: High-Quality Demonstration Collection
To improve demonstration quality, which is vital for imitation learning, the operator holds physical tools matching those on the robot. The user grasps a knife-shaped device to move the knife, and a tong-shaped device to move the tongs. This eliminates unnatural control mappings and enables intuitive teleoperation. The 6-DoF pose of the tool is tracked by an Intel RealSense T265 tracking camera, and tong opening/closing is detected via the relative angle of two IMUs (inertial measurement units). All data (multi-camera RGB images, tactile signals, joint states, actions) are collected in strict synchronization at 20Hz, and a real-time tactile map is overlaid on the screen.

### II-D Policy Learning: From Demonstrations to Long-Horizon Tasks
To execute long-horizon tasks, a hierarchical policy is employed. The high-level tool selection policy $\pi_{\text{sel}}$ takes the overhead workspace image $\mathcal{O}_{top}$ and goal image $\mathcal{O}_{g}$ as inputs, outputting a probability distribution over the next tool to use via a ResNet and MLP. Once the tool is selected and swapped, a tool-specific low-level control policy $\pi_{\text{tool}}$ is activated. The control policy uses a U-Net-based Diffusion Policy to generate smooth end-effector actions conditioned on multi-view images, tactile signals, and robot joint states. When the change in end-effector position remains below 0.005m for 20 consecutive steps, the skill is determined to be complete, and the robot resets to the home position to transition to the next tool selection.

sections.heading: The Power of Touch: Easing Teleoperation and Boosting Imitation Learning
sections.summary: After identifying a 2mm electrode width as optimal for the tactile sensor, a 12-participant teleoperation study confirmed improved task efficiency and reduced operator workload. Furthermore, in the pan-fried tofu cooking task, incorporating touch into the policy boosted success rates by up to 25 percentage points.
sections.details:
The experiments evaluated three aspects: tactile sensor characterization, teleoperation usability, and real-robot imitation learning policy performance.

### III-A Characterization of Tool-Specific Tactile Sensors
Experiments on a testbed evaluated varying electrode widths for the pressure-sensitive sensor. Larger electrode areas increase sensitivity, but when load is applied, the signal spikes rapidly, saturating the 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC). Conversely, overly small electrodes lack sufficient sensitivity. Evaluating this trade-off led to adopting 2mm-wide electrodes, which provide smooth continuous readings and retain an adequate measurement range.

### III-B Evaluation of Tool-Centric Teleoperation
A user study with 12 participants (novice, intermediate, and expert) was conducted across two tasks: brushing and knife cutting. Three conditions were compared: (1) a generic VR-controller-style tool, (2) SwapBot without tactile visualization, and (3) SwapBot with real-time on-screen tactile feedback. Metrics included completion time, success rate, and subjective workload via NASA-TLX. Across all proficiency levels, SwapBot reduced completion time and increased success rates. Notably, with tactile visualization, cognitive workload (mental workload) was lowest because the moment of contact and changes in load were clearly visible.

### III-C Long-Horizon Policy Learning with Tactile Feedback
The real-world task evaluated was "cooking pan-fried tofu." The task consists of three demanding stages: (1) delicately brushing sauce onto fragile tofu, (2) grasping it with tongs to move it to a pan for cooking, and (3) returning it to the cutting board and cleanly slicing it in half with a knife. For each stage, 100 teleoperation demonstrations were collected to train policies.
Comparing tool success rates, the proposed method incorporating tactile signals significantly outperformed the RGB-only baseline. Success rates reached 85% for brushing (vs. 65% for RGB-only), 70% for tong grasping (vs. 50% for RGB-only), and 90% for knife cutting (vs. 75% for RGB-only). With RGB only, occlusions prevented seeing the exact moment the tong tips touched the tofu or early signs of slippage, frequently resulting in crushed or dropped tofu. Furthermore, tactile benefits were even more pronounced in low-data regimes, maintaining high success rates with fewer demonstrations with statistical significance ($p < 0.05$).
The high-level tool selector achieved a 96.8% classification accuracy on the test set, and the fully autonomous execution across the entire chained cooking task reached a 60% success rate. Even when perturbations occurred, such as manually shifting the tofu's position mid-task, the visuo-tactile policy demonstrated robustness by re-approaching and continuing the task.

sections.heading: Tracing Tool Manipulation, Swapping Mechanisms, and Tactile Sensing
sections.summary: Unlike prior work focused on learning how to grasp tools, this work uniquely transforms everyday tools directly into tactile end effectors. It overcomes the high cost of industrial changers and the bulkiness of GelSight sensors by achieving low-cost, slim tactile integration.
sections.details:
Related work spans three main domains:

### IV-A Robotic Tool Manipulation
Much prior research on robotic tool use (such as RoboCook) has focused on affordance learning and task-oriented grasping—determining where to grasp a tool. However, grasping a tool handle with a generic gripper often allows the tool to slip or rotate in hand under heavy loads, making forceful tasks like cutting difficult to execute stably. In contrast, SwapBot directly converts the tool itself into a rigidly coupled end effector rather than grasping it, mechanically eliminating fundamental issues such as tool re-grasping and grasp slippage.

### IV-B Hardware Design for Tool Use
Industrial robot tool changers offer high rigidity and precision, but are very expensive and struggle to support tools requiring external actuation like tongs. Additionally, surgical robot instrument swapping mechanisms have been explored, but are not intended for household settings. SwapBot introduces novelty by handling both passive and articulated tools through a unified interface at an ultra-low cost of under $10.

### IV-C Tactile Sensing for Manipulation
In robotic touch, optical tactile sensors using cameras and silicone elastomer (such as GelSight) are well known, but their bulky form factor makes embedding them into tool tips or thin handles difficult. Conversely, tactile skins using piezoresistive or capacitive sheets offer slim profiles and flexible custom shaping. SwapBot adopts this approach, custom-fabricating sensors to fit tool geometries via digital fabrication to acquire crucial contact forces at the exact moment of interaction without obstructing operations.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways and What Lies Ahead
sections.summary: SwapBot demonstrates a practical pathway for contact-rich everyday tasks by pairing tool interchangeability with tactile sensing. Future directions include improving sensor durability and achieving end-to-end autonomy via automated subgoal generation.
sections.details:
This paper presented SwapBot, a system that converts everyday tools into tactile end effectors using low-cost modular adapters. Intuitive, tool-matched teleoperation interfaces enable high-quality demonstration collection, and imitation learning incorporating tactile feedback proved capable of high success rates even on delicate, fragile tasks like cooking tofu.

At the same time, the authors acknowledge several limitations:
- The tactile sensors have low resolution and face concerns regarding wear and degradation over long-term use.
- Sensor placement locations are currently fixed based on human intuition rather than automated optimization.
- For overall task execution, subgoal definitions (intermediate goal images) and task transitions are manually configured.

Future work points to introducing more durable, higher-resolution sensing technologies, automatically determining optimal sensor placement in a data-driven manner, and developing fully autonomous policy sequencing that eliminates manual subgoal definitions. To facilitate reproducibility and adoption in the robotics community, the system hardware and code have been released open source.

takeaways: Swapping low-cost tools is far more practical than building a universal multi-fingered hand in terms of mechanical reliability, cost, and ease of control.

In contact-rich tasks (cutting, grasping, spreading), feeding tactile signals placed on tool tips and handles alongside RGB images dramatically boosts imitation learning data efficiency and robustness.
Equipping teleoperators with the same tools as the robot and displaying real-time tactile visualizations substantially lowers cognitive workload, leading to higher-quality demonstration data.
limitations: Custom piezoresistive film sensors have low resolution and are vulnerable to wear and degradation from repeated friction and heavy loads.
Where tactile sensors are attached on each tool relies on designer intuition, lacking automated optimization tailored to specific tasks.
Long-horizon task decomposition and intermediate subgoal image sequences are manually predefined, falling short of fully automated planning and failure recovery.
